thread.title: Starbucks: 2.7% Yield And 20% Dividend Growth - Starbucks Corporation (NASDAQ:SBUX)

author: Nicholas Ward
title: Starbucks: 2.7% Yield And 20% Dividend Growth - Starbucks Corporation (NASDAQ:SBUX)
text:
When Starbucks ( SBUX ) announced disappointing guidance after hours on Tuesday, I knew the stock would be in for a rough ride Wednesday. Analysts had factored in ~3% growth into their estimates and news that same store comps were going to be in the ~1% range during the upcoming quarter was surely disappointing news. What's more, these declining comps fit into a longer term narrative regarding SBUX's slowing growth that has kept the shares range bound for several years now.
I've written about this several times already, but it seems clear now that we're witnessing one of the great growth companies of our time transform into a value name. That doesn't mean that SBUX can't be a great value holding. What it does mean is that it will take time a bit of time for the market to smooth out the valuation wrinkles.
While SBUX did disappoint with same store sales growth, it's important to acknowledge that the company increased its dividend by 20%. SBUX management paired the bad news with very good news that it plans on returning ~$25b to shareholders in the form of dividends and buybacks by FY2020.
This is the fate of just about every growth company in the market as they mature, though I think many investors have been holding out hope that Chinese market penetration would continue to fuel SBUX's growth engine for years to come. I've been somewhat skeptical of that bullish trend, which is why I trimmed my SBUX position earlier in the year. I was content to have less exposure to SBUX because of slowing growth concerns, though today's ~10% drop has sparked my interest again and now I'm strongly considering buying back the shares that I sold at a significant discount.
It's never fun for investors when a company transitions from value to growth. Best case scenario, we see sideways movement as the multiple compresses over time, and worst case, we end up seeing negative share price movement if the market isn't as patient with the compression process. Thus far, the market has given SBUX the benefit of the doubt with regard to its premium multiple. However, it appears that with Howard Schultz gone, that dam broke a bit on Tuesday, with the market moving to a more show-me state of mind now that CEO Kevin Johnson is running the show solo.
On the F.A.S.T. Graph below you can see SBUX's consolidation over the last couple of years closely. Fundamental growth has continued, but the share price has moved sideways as SBUX's premium has fallen from ~30x ttm to ~20x ttm. There's no telling how long this will continue or how low the market will let the stock's valuation slide before it puts a bid under the shares. I think a ~18x valuation makes sense for SBUX moving forward, though the market has a habit of placing much higher valuations on names like this (McDonald's (NYSE: MCD ), for instance, always seems to trade with a higher premium than I'd like to pay) and therefore, I wouldn't be surprised if SBUX found support in the ~20x range (which essentially coincides with its 52-week low) and isn't all that far from Tuesday's bottom. It's worth noting that SBUX hasn't traded for less than 20x ttm since 2010, so we're close to entering recently uncharted territory with this weakness.
Source: F.A.S.T. Graphs
The days of double digit top-line growth are likely behind SBUX. In the U.S. stores are possible too highly concentrated, which is why management is shutting some down. Personally, I don't mind the move to shutter underperforming stores. Any location that is a drag on profitability is a problem. A focus on margins/profitability instead of revenue growth is likely going to be a good thing for more conservative, income oriented investors. I've heard Starbucks referred to as the McDonald's of the Millennial generation.
At this point in time, I think that is an apt comparison. To me, the focus for SBUX should no longer be on the top line, but instead, the bottom. Growth will continue to come from international markets where the company is under penetrated, but at this point in time of the company's life cycle, I think it's fair for the market to place a more Staples-esque multiple on SBUX shares and focus primarily on shareholder returns.
I've held this mindset for awhile now. I've written before about my concerns regarding SBUX's premium multiple. It seemed unlikely that SBUX would have been able to produce the growth necessary to justify a ~25x multiple, though I maintained an overweight position for years because the company's dividend growth was simply too much to ignore. Earlier in the year, I finally decided to reduce my exposure a bit. I sold ~30% of my SBUX shares at $58.83 and put the proceeds to use buying Honeywell (NYSE: HON ) at $150.42.
Both stocks are down a bit, but thankfully, HON has performed better on a relative basis. Honeywell is a best in breed company, in my opinion, yet it has gotten caught up the industrial sell-off with tariffs/trade war news sparking concerns of slower growth and the likelihood of a sweeping infrastructure bill domestically being diminished as the Trump administration seems to have shifted its focused to trade overseas. I'm happy to own a larger HON position. HON shares have a similar yield to SBUX and while their dividend growth prospects aren't quite as rosy on a relative basis in the short-term, over the long-term, I think HON can give investors double digit annual increases, which is exactly what I want to see from shares with dividend yields in the 2.5% range.
Trade related issues with China helped to inspire this trade. It seemed obvious to me that China was one of the few growth levers that SBUX had left to pull and although Starbucks management has made inroads with the Chinese government throughout their expansion into that country, I still have fears/doubts regarding the reliability of returns coming from that market over the long-term due to the communist regime and the oppressive control that the government has on the "private" sector there.
This remains a threat. Maybe SBUX will be forced to go the Yum! (NYSE: YUM ) route and spin off its Chinese operations. This wouldn't be good for the company since it continues to highlight China as its primary growth driver, yet I don't want to spend too much time speculating about that sort of interference by the Chinese government. Instead, I'll say that I'm willing to put the risks aside and potentially increase my exposure to SBUX.
So, when thinking about buying SBUX shares, I have a few options with regard to where the funds will come from. I'll discuss the options that I considered throughout the day Tuesday, fishing for some feedback. I decided to give this sell-off a couple of days and hopefully letting the dust settle a bit before buying into it. I wouldn't be surprised to see if SBUX tests the $50 threshold (~20x current 2018 estimates) and I wanted to see if that would hold. Waiting a few days gives me time to plan out the trade, rather than making a rash decision. So, without further adieu, here are my options when it comes to making room for more SBUX in my portfolio.
My first option, which is probably the simplest, is to dip into my cash position. Cash makes up ~10% of my portfolio at the moment. However, I'd rather not dip into that stockpile because my wife is still in graduate school for another 9 months or so and I like having it as a windfall for big bills/mortgage payments during months when my income isn't enough to cover all the necessities on its own.
What's more, I believe we're operating in a late cycle environment and while SBUX trading down ~10% is an attractive dip, I think we could see a recession brewing in the next year or two (the yield curve is getting very flat and could potentially invert in the next 6 months or so) and that would present even better deals. Thankfully, it typically takes a year or so after the yield curve inverts for a recession to really take hold and my wife should be back to work by then. Once she re-enters the work force we'll have the ability to save/invest with a much larger household income than we have at the moment. Either way, playing the guessing game with macro trends like that is very tricky business and I like the idea of maintaining a respectable stock of dry powder on hand in case a black swan event turns the markets much sooner than I expect.
So, assuming that I don't dip into cash, I'm going to have to sell something to raise funds for a SBUX purchase. I don't have any low hanging fruit in my portfolio anymore, meaning that a cut somewhere is going to be a hard decision.
First things first, Royal Caribbean ( RCL ) came to mind. This is one of my most recent purchases , made on May 29th. I bought RCL at $105.42 and in just a few weeks, the stock has shot up nearly 6%. I thought RCL was undervalued when I bought it and I continue to think so, but I also don't believe that RCL represents the same sort of quality as SBUX in terms of dividend growth. RCL cut its dividend during the Great Recession and while I believe that the company is much stronger today than it was back then, I still acknowledge the fact that RCL is highly dependent on a healthy consumer and will likely do very poorly during the next bear market. After recent weakness, SBUX has a much higher yield than RCL (~2.7% compared to ~2.1%). I do expect a dividend increase from RCL in the coming months which will help to close that gap, but either way, trading in RCL for SBUX would definitely increase my passive income.
Some other companies that I'm considering selling to raise cash for SBUX are the big banks in my portfolio. I also recently wrote about these companies, touting them as attractive dividend growth names ahead of the CCAR results that we'll begin to see later this week. Last year the CCAR results opened the door for massive dividend/buyback announcements and I expect more of the same this year. However, I don't think that any of these banks can compete with SBUX in terms of dividend growth over the long-term and like RCL, they represent higher risks in the event of a bear market.
When I make trades I pay attention to three main things. One, I hate losing money so I always like to sell winners and lock in profits rather than losses. Two, I hate paying fees so I make sure that I do this in a tax efficient way. And three, I like to increase my passive income stream when I'm actively managing my portfolio. In other words, I don't like selling company and using the proceeds to buy something that yields less. With these three thoughts in mind, I arrived at the Chinese internet names that I own.
I'm up big in Alibaba ( BABA ) and Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ) and I have slight gains in JD.com ( JD ) and Baidu ( BIDU ). None of these names generate meaningful income for my portfolio and I hold them all in IRA accounts, so selling them to make room for SBUX would check all of my boxes. However, I really like these names long -term. I think they offer much higher growth prospects than SBUX, while admittedly adding increased risks and volatility to my holdings. I'm not sure if I really want to lose the growth that they offer, but if I can't figure out something else to cut to make room for a beaten down SBUX, these names become easy ATM machines for me to tap into.
Another portfolio management strategy that I like to use is owning both sides of a duopoly. Rather than pick favorites when it comes to high quality pairs, I simply buy them both (usually at the same time). I'm talking about the Coca-Colas ( KO ) and Pepsis (NYSE: PEP ) of the world. The Visas ( V ) and Mastercards ( MA ). The AT&Ts ( T ) and Verizons ( VZ ). The Disneys ( DIS ) and Comcasts ( CMCSA ). You get the picture. I like this strategy because oftentimes I believe its better to have broader exposure to my favorite industries than attempt to pick winners and losers.
Well, in one of my favorite industries, logistics, this strategy is breaking down a bit, because while I own both FedEx ( FDX ) and United Parcel Service ( UPS ), it's becoming clear to me that this is more of a one horse race. Today, if you were to ask me, I'd say that FedEx is well ahead of UPS in terms of quality. With this in mind, I don't feel as compelled to own both companies and I could take profits on UPS to raise cash for SBUX. UPS's yield is slightly higher than SBUX's at the moment, meaning that I wouldn't quite check all of my boxes with this trade, but the yield gap isn't all that wide and because of SBUX's much greater dividend growth prospects, I imagine that it wouldn't take very long for SBUX shares bought at these levels to surpass UPS in terms of the size of the passive income generated within my portfolio.
I recently wrote about my belief that Nike ( NKE ) overvalued. I said that I wasn't interested in selling my shares quite yet because I didn't see a suitable replacement within the same quality tier. There aren't very many dividend growth stocks that can stack up to Nike, but I think Starbucks is one of them. Selling/trimming my Nike stake starts to make sense on a relative valuation basis as SBUX sells off. Nike is currently trading for ~27.5x forward earnings while SBUX is trading for only ~20x its 2019 estimates. Nike's growth prospects are better than SBUX's, but SBUX's yield is much higher. This trade is a real possibility.
And lastly, I come to another potential high quality swap: Apple ( AAPL ) for Starbucks. AAPL is by far my largest position and therefore, it's a relatively easy place to go to when I need to raise cash. I don't like the idea of selling AAPL shares because its probably my favorite long-term dividend growth holding, but SBUX shares aren't too shabby either and this trade would drastically increase my passive income in the short-term. I recently purchased some AAPL shares at $157.53 on a dip in my IRA and I could take advantage of the unexpected ~18% pop to raise raise some quick cash and make room for extra SBUX shares. Even if I sold these shares, AAPL would still be my largest holding. I don't think that this is my best option, but then again, AAPL is getting a bit top heavy at ~8.4% of my portfolio and I wouldn't mind reducing that exposure level a bit over time.
So, what do you think? If you were in my shoes, which trade would you make for Starbucks? Or, maybe I'm over complicating things a bit here and the correct answer is to see how this sell-off shakes out a bit and do nothing at all. Time will tell, but in the meantime, I always appreciate input from the Seeking Alpha community.
Disclosure: I am/we are long SBUX, RCL, AAPL, DIS, CMCSA, KO, PEP, VZ, T, NKE, BABA, JD, TCEHY, BIDU, MA, V, FDX, UPS.
